body:
What is an earthquake?

An earthquake is the sudden shaking of the Earth's surface caused by the rapid release of energy within the Earth. Most damaging natural earthquakes occur when rocks break or slip along a fault, releasing energy that travels through the Earth as seismic waves.

The Earth's outer rigid layer, called the lithosphere, is divided into tectonic plates. These plates move slowly relative to one another. Their movement creates stresses in the rocks of the Earth's crust. When accumulated stress exceeds the strength of rocks along a fault, sudden movement occurs and an earthquake is generated.

Earthquakes are classified as endogenic phenomena because the forces responsible for them originate within the Earth. They may occur near plate boundaries or along faults within a tectonic plate.

Earthquake hazard is the potential for damaging earthquake effects at a location. Earthquake risk concerns the possible losses when that hazard affects exposed and vulnerable people, buildings and infrastructure.

Focus, epicentre and seismic waves

The point within the Earth where earthquake rupture begins is called the focus or hypocentre. The point on the Earth's surface vertically above the focus is the epicentre.

Seismic energy travels outward from the earthquake source. The principal seismic waves are:

  • Primary waves or P-waves: These are compressional waves and generally arrive first at a seismic recording station.
  • Secondary waves or S-waves: These produce shear motion, travel more slowly than P-waves and do not pass through liquids.
  • Surface waves: These travel along the Earth's surface and can contribute substantially to damaging ground movement.

The greatest damage is often concentrated near the earthquake source, but actual damage also depends on the depth of the earthquake, local soil conditions, distance from the rupture and strength of buildings. The epicentre is therefore not necessarily the location of the greatest destruction.

Magnitude and intensity are different

Two terms are especially important when interpreting earthquake information.

ConceptMeaningImportant distinction
MagnitudeMeasures the size of the earthquake at its source.A single earthquake has one magnitude estimate on a specified magnitude scale, subject to scientific revision.
IntensityDescribes the severity of shaking and its observed effects at a particular location.Intensity can differ from place to place during the same earthquake.

The Richter scale, or local magnitude scale, is commonly mentioned in school textbooks. For large earthquakes, scientists frequently report moment magnitude (Mw), which estimates earthquake size from the seismic moment. Both are magnitude measures, but they are not identical measurement methods.

Intensity scales include the Modified Mercalli Intensity scale and the Medvedev-Sponheuer-Karnik (MSK) scale. These describe shaking effects rather than the total size of the earthquake.

Why an earthquake becomes a disaster

An earthquake does not automatically produce a disaster. Its consequences depend on the interaction between the earthquake hazard and the conditions of the affected area.

  • Hazard: The possibility and severity of damaging ground shaking or related ground failure.
  • Exposure: People, houses, schools, hospitals, roads and other assets located where shaking may occur.
  • Vulnerability: Conditions that make exposed people or assets susceptible to damage, such as weak buildings or inadequate preparedness.
  • Capacity: The ability of communities and institutions to reduce damage, protect people and recover.

For example, strong shaking in an uninhabited area may cause little direct human loss. The same shaking in a densely populated town with poorly constructed buildings may cause extensive destruction. Safer construction, retrofitting and preparedness can reduce losses even though the earthquake hazard itself remains.

Gujarat provides an important example because the state contains highly earthquake-prone regions, particularly Kachchh, as well as densely populated urban and rural settlements with different building vulnerabilities.

Prelims focus

  • Earthquakes are generally caused by sudden fault movement and the release of stored strain energy.
  • The focus is inside the Earth; the epicentre is directly above it on the surface.
  • P-waves generally arrive before S-waves.
  • Magnitude describes earthquake size; intensity describes effects at a location.
  • Earthquake risk depends on hazard, exposure, vulnerability and capacity.
  • Trap: High earthquake magnitude does not mean identical shaking or damage at every location.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7 Geography, Chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed pp. 12–14, 2018–19 printing; NCERT, Science, Class 8, Chapter 15, Some Natural Phenomena, printed pp. 191–195, 2018–19 printing; National Disaster Management Authority, National Disaster Management Guidelines: Management of Earthquakes, April 2007, Chapter 1, pp. 7–13.]

title: Understanding Earthquakes and Earthquake Risk in Gujarat

body:
The tectonic setting of Gujarat

Gujarat lies in western India, within the broader region influenced by the continuing movement of the Indian tectonic plate. The Indian plate is moving relative to the Eurasian plate, and the resulting stresses affect a large region of the subcontinent.

The Himalayan region experiences intense seismic activity because of the convergence of the Indian and Eurasian plates. However, damaging earthquakes are not restricted to the immediate Himalayan plate boundary. Stresses can also reactivate ancient faults located within the Indian plate.

Kachchh is an important intraplate earthquake region. An intraplate earthquake occurs within a tectonic plate rather than directly on the principal boundary between 2 plates.

Kachchh contains an old rift-related geological structure with several faults. Although these structures originated in an earlier geological setting, some remain capable of movement under present-day regional stresses. The 2001 Bhuj earthquake demonstrated that a major earthquake can occur within the Indian plate.

Important distinction: Gujarat's seismic activity is influenced by stresses associated with Indian plate movement, but the 2001 Bhuj earthquake did not occur directly on the surface boundary between the Indian and Eurasian plates. It was an intraplate earthquake involving faulting within the Indian plate.

Historical earthquakes in Kachchh

The history of damaging earthquakes confirms that seismic risk in Kachchh is not limited to the event of 2001.

YearEarthquakeSignificance
1819Rann of Kachchh earthquakeA major historical earthquake associated with substantial ground deformation.
1956Anjar earthquakeA damaging earthquake that demonstrated continuing seismic activity in Kachchh.
2001Bhuj or Kachchh earthquakeA major intraplate earthquake that caused extensive destruction across Gujarat.

These events demonstrate that a region can experience repeated damaging earthquakes even when long intervals separate major events. The absence of a recent large earthquake does not establish that a location is free from seismic hazard.

Seismic zones of Gujarat

The Bureau of Indian Standards (BIS) divides India into seismic zones for earthquake-resistant structural design. Under the seismic zoning associated with IS 1893 (Part 1):2016, India has 4 zones: II, III, IV and V.

Zone V represents the highest seismic hazard category in this classification, while Zone II represents the lowest.

Seismic zoneRelative hazardGujarat connection
VVery highKachchh, including the Rann of Kachchh region.
IVHighParts of Jamnagar, Rajkot, Patan and Banaskantha districts.
IIIModerateMost of the remaining parts of Gujarat.
IILowerA very small part of Gujarat in the state authority's published description.

These are broad regional descriptions. A district may include more than 1 seismic zone; the precise classification of an individual site must be established from the applicable official map rather than inferred from the district name alone.

Seismic zones must not be confused with the actual intensity experienced during a particular earthquake. A zone indicates a regional design-hazard category. Actual shaking during an earthquake depends on its source, distance, depth and local geological conditions.

Seismic zoning and microzonation

Seismic zonation identifies broad regions according to their expected earthquake hazard. Seismic microzonation examines smaller areas in greater detail to identify local differences in shaking and ground-failure potential.

Two localities within the same broad seismic zone may experience different shaking because of their soil deposits, underlying rock and geological conditions.

For example, loose sediment deposits may amplify certain ground motions compared with nearby hard-rock locations. Where loose, water-saturated sandy soil is subjected to strong shaking, liquefaction may occur. In liquefaction, soil temporarily loses much of its strength and stiffness, potentially causing settlement, tilting or damage to structures.

Liquefaction is a consequence of earthquake shaking under susceptible ground conditions; it is not the cause of the tectonic earthquake.

Gujarat's Institute of Seismological Research undertakes seismic hazard assessment, site studies and microzonation. Such studies help improve land-use planning, construction decisions and the identification of vulnerable settlements.

Prelims focus

  • Kachchh is a major intraplate seismic region of India.
  • Major historical earthquakes include the Rann of Kachchh earthquake of 1819 and the Anjar earthquake of 1956.
  • Under the 2016 seismic zoning framework, India has Zones II, III, IV and V.
  • Kachchh lies in Zone V, the highest seismic hazard category.
  • Seismic microzonation examines local variations in ground conditions and earthquake hazard.
  • Trap: A seismic zone does not represent the intensity that must occur during every earthquake.

[References: Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Earthquake, sections on seismic zoning and historical earthquakes, accessed 2 November 2026; U.S. Geological Survey, The Mw 7.7 Bhuj Earthquake: Global Lessons for Earthquake Hazard in Intra-Plate Regions, 2003, abstract; Press Information Bureau, Ministry of Earth Sciences, Parliament Question: Seismograph Network, 1 April 2026; Institute of Seismological Research, Seismic Hazard Assessment and Microzonation Group, accessed 2 November 2026.]

title: Why Kachchh Is Highly Earthquake-Prone: Tectonics, Faults and Seismic Zones

body:
The earthquake of 26 January 2001

On 26 January 2001, Gujarat experienced one of the most destructive earthquakes in modern Indian history. The earthquake occurred at approximately 8:46 a.m. Indian Standard Time, on Republic Day.

It is commonly called the Bhuj earthquake or the Kachchh earthquake. The name Bhuj should not be understood to mean that the earthquake's epicentre was located inside Bhuj city. The epicentral area lay farther east in Kachchh, near the Bhachau region.

The United States Geological Survey records the earthquake as moment magnitude Mw 7.7. Its event catalogue identifies shallow oblique reverse faulting within the continental crust of the Indian plate. Reverse faulting involves movement in which the rock mass above an inclined fault moves upward relative to the rock mass below it, reflecting compression.

Magnitude reporting: Different publications report different values for the 2001 earthquake because they use different magnitude estimates or historical reporting conventions. The USGS event catalogue reports Mw 7.7, while a GSDMA information page gives 7.6. An older NCERT case-study headline gives 6.9. For a precise scientific statement, identify the source and magnitude scale; do not treat all published values as directly interchangeable.

Extent of the destruction

The most severely affected locations included parts of Kachchh such as Bhuj, Bhachau and Anjar. Damage also occurred in other parts of Gujarat, including Ahmedabad, demonstrating that damaging earthquake effects can extend far beyond the immediate epicentral area.

GSDMA's seismic microzonation information reports more than 13,800 deaths and approximately 170,000 injuries from the disaster. These are retrospective figures reported by that authority, not estimates of present earthquake risk.

The earthquake caused several kinds of damage:

  • Residential buildings: Many traditional masonry houses and inadequately designed reinforced-concrete buildings suffered severe damage or collapse.
  • Public buildings: Damage to schools, hospitals and other facilities disrupted education, healthcare and essential services.
  • Transport and utilities: Damage to roads, bridges, electricity systems, water supply and communications complicated relief and recovery.
  • Ground failure: Liquefaction, ground cracking and other ground failures affected susceptible locations.
  • Livelihoods: Families lost homes, workplaces, business assets and sources of income.

What the earthquake revealed about buildings

Investigations of the Bhuj earthquake established an important distinction: the material used in a building does not, by itself, determine whether the building is earthquake-resistant.

Traditional brick, stone and other masonry buildings were particularly vulnerable where walls lacked adequate connections, roofs were heavy or construction quality was poor.

Some reinforced-concrete buildings also failed. Important contributing factors included inadequate earthquake-resistant detailing, poor construction practices, irregular building layouts and weak ground floors.

A notable problem was the open-ground-storey building, commonly constructed with parking space at ground level and masonry-filled floors above. Such buildings may have a sudden reduction in lateral stiffness and strength at ground level. Without appropriate engineering, shaking can concentrate damage in that weaker storey.

The experience therefore established that seismic safety requires suitable structural design, sound construction practices, compliance with applicable standards and attention to local ground conditions.

From emergency relief to long-term risk reduction

The disaster also exposed the importance of coordinated administration, reliable communications, community preparedness and safe public infrastructure.

The Government of Gujarat established the Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority (GSDMA) on 8 February 2001 to coordinate the extensive recovery programme. Gujarat subsequently enacted the Gujarat State Disaster Management Act, 2003, providing a statutory framework for disaster management in the state.

Reconstruction extended beyond replacing damaged houses. It included restoration of infrastructure, support for livelihoods, capacity building, preparedness and measures to reduce future disaster losses. Owner-driven housing reconstruction, supported by technical guidance and staged assistance, became an important part of the recovery approach.

Lasting lessons

The earthquake established that reducing earthquake disaster losses requires action before the next major event. Important lessons include improving the safety of existing buildings, enforcing safer construction standards, protecting essential facilities and developing effective local disaster-management capacity.

It also demonstrated that immediate rescue and relief are necessary but insufficient. Rehabilitation must restore community functioning, and reconstruction should reduce the vulnerabilities that caused earlier losses.

Prelims focus

  • The Bhuj earthquake occurred on 26 January 2001 at approximately 8:46 a.m. IST.
  • The USGS records a moment magnitude of Mw 7.7.
  • It was an intraplate earthquake involving reverse faulting within the Indian plate.
  • Important affected places included Bhuj, Bhachau, Anjar and Ahmedabad.
  • GSDMA was established on 8 February 2001.
  • The Gujarat State Disaster Management Act was enacted in 2003.

[References: U.S. Geological Survey, earthquake event usp000a8ds, Event Summary and Tectonic Summary, accessed 2 November 2026; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Feasibility Study on Seismic Microzonation and Constitution and History, accessed 2 November 2026; Indian Institute of Technology Kanpur, National Information Center of Earthquake Engineering, The 2001 Bhuj Earthquake, Introduction and Reinforced Concrete Buildings; Gujarat State Disaster Management Authority, Gujarat Earthquake Rehabilitation and Reconstruction Policy, introduction; NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7 Geography, Chapter 3, Our Changing Earth, printed p. 14, 2018–19 printing.]
